sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's standard library database/sql package is the foundation for all relational database access in Go. Unlike higher-level ORMs, it exposes connection pooling, prepared statement caching, and transaction semantics directly to the developer. Interviewers probe this module to verify you understand the lifecycle of a sql.DB (not a single connection — it is a pool), why rows.Close() is mandatory, and how sqlx layered on top of database/sql reduces scan boilerplate without hiding the SQL itself. Mastery here signals you can write performant, correct, production-grade data access code.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Think of sql.DB as a managed pool of TCP connections to your database. sql.Open() registers the driver and configures the pool but does NOT open any connections — use db.PingContext() to verify connectivity. Every call to db.Query() or db.QueryRow() borrows a connection from the pool, runs the query, and the connection is returned only when rows.Close() is called (or the *Row scan completes). sqlx wraps sql.DB and adds StructScan, NamedQuery, and In() helpers that map database columns directly to exported struct fields via db struct tags, removing the manual rows.Scan(&a, &b, &c) repetition.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. sql.Open vs db.PingContext — Open does not connect, Ping verifies the pool. 2. SetMaxOpenConns / SetMaxIdleConns / SetConnMaxLifetime — three levers that control pool behaviour; idle > open is wasteful, too-short lifetime causes churn. 3. rows.Close() must always be deferred after checking the error from Query(); without it the connection is leaked. 4. db.QueryRow returns a *Row; the error surfaces at .Scan(), not at QueryRow(). 5. db.Prepare caches a statement server-side; use it when executing the same query thousands of times per second. 6. db.Begin / tx.Commit / tx.Rollback — always defer a rollback as a safety net even if you call Commit. 7. sqlx.NamedQuery uses :param placeholders and a struct or map, avoiding positional argument bugs. 8. sqlx.StructScan and sqlx.Select map column names to struct fields via the db tag.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What is sql.DB and why is it safe to share globally? — It is a thread-safe connection pool, not a single connection. Q: What happens if you forget rows.Close()? — The connection is never returned to the pool; under load you exhaust SetMaxOpenConns and new queries block or time out. Q: When would you use db.Prepare vs inline Query? — Prepare for hot-path repeated queries to avoid per-call parse/plan overhead on the DB server. Q: How does sqlx.NamedQuery prevent positional argument bugs? — Parameters are referenced by name (:user_id) not position, so reordering struct fields does not break the query. Q: How do you handle a transaction that might be committed or rolled back depending on business logic? — defer tx.Rollback() immediately after Begin; it is a no-op if Commit already succeeded.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "In production I treat sql.DB as a long-lived singleton configured at startup. I always set MaxOpenConns equal to the database's max_connections divided by the number of service replicas, and I set ConnMaxLifetime to something like 5 minutes to handle mid-air database failovers. I defer rows.Close() right after checking the query error — that's the most common leak I've caught in code reviews. For ad-hoc queries I use sqlx.StructScan because it eliminates a whole class of column-order bugs; but I still write raw SQL so the execution plan is explicit and reviewable. For transactions I defer a rollback immediately after Begin, which acts as a safety net — it's a no-op if the function reaches Commit successfully."
